newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Nov 14.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Nov 14.

text.p: THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Contradicting comments made by Prime Minister John Howard that the Government's media review would end up looking at foreign ownership limits, Communications Minister Richard Alston said yesterday the review would only explore changes to the cross-ownershp limits between newspapers and television. Page 1.

Although he approved a fresh application from Christopher Skase's bankruptcy trustee, Max Donnelly, for additional funding to investigate the prospect of recovering the Spain-based fugitive's assets, Federal Attorney-General Daryl Williams said yesterday he did not have great expectations of any significant recovery of assets. Page 2.

The Federal Government is considering a proposal to place a levy of between half to one cent on telephone calls for a period of between two to three years to fund the burial of all aerial cables underground. The plan would depend on the Commonwealth receiving support from the States , local Governments, telecommunications carriers and power companies. Page 3.

Claiming yesterday that Aborigines wanted to break away from the dependency mentality, Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron will tomorrow unveil a new plan to enlist the help of the Australian Army to construct infrastructure, such as water and sewerage projects, as part of a drive to improve health and conditions in remote Aboriginal communities. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Federal Attorney-General Daryl Williams signalled yesterday the Government's intention to reverse the trend toward an interventionist High Court, claiming politically-contentious issues are best handled by Parliament as part of the political process, not by the court. Williams also foreshadowed a renewed move towards the introduction of uniform defamation laws. Page 1.

If West Australian Premier Richard Court announces an early State election today, his immediate shift to a "caretaker" role would stop him from committing his State to any decisions made at the Council of Australian Governments meeting in Brisbane, schedued for tomorrow. If the COAG meeting is cancelled as a result of the election, Court could save himself from electoral harm, as he is a strong advocate of tax reform, including the goods and services tax, which is set to be a key issue on the COAG agenda Page 1.

Amid threats of industrial action by New South Wales police over the unprecedented powers granted to Police Commissioner Peter Ryan, Ryan revealed yesterday he was drawing up a list of officers he intended to sack after they were exposed as corrupt by the New South Wales Police Royal Commission. Ryan said his powers to hire and fire officers were essential to the reform of the service. Page 3.

After labelling conditions in the Children's Court an "utter disgrace", Victorian Chief Magistrate Michael Adams QC yesterday called for the establishment of "diversion programs" to reduce the number of children and mentally disabled people going through the court system. Adams said the Magistrates Court had no way of adequately dealing with crimes committed by people with intellectual disabilities and they were entitled to an adequate system of justice. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Federal Government is set to mobilise Australian Army engineers to provide water supplies to 280 Aboriginal communities which still have no running water or basic sewerage, despite opposition from military chiefs to the idea of Defence Force personnelcarrying out a large-scale civilian task. Aboriginal Social Justice Commissioner Mick Dodson said the plan was a return to the mission days and "has the stench of whitey knows best for black fellas". Page 1.

There is hope that scientists have found a more powerful and more specific drug than tamoxifen, the leading breast cancer drug, after early results from a trial of the experimental drug Faalodex, a synthetic oestrogen blocker, showed that nearly 70 per cet of the 19 women with advanced breast cancer had either complete remission of their cancer or the tumours stopped growing. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard is receiving conflicting advise over whether to lobby US President Bill Clinton for his support to stop a United States trade move which could cost thousands of Australian jobs. Senior trade and industry officials are urging Howard to warn Clinton that the action could seriously damage relations between Australia and the US, but the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade says Clinton can do nothing to stop the trade action and Howard would do better to concentrate on broader stategic issues when Clinton arrives in Australia next week. Page 1.

Maintaining the child-sex charge against him was contrived, former Ambassador to Cambodia John Holloway said yesterday he looked forward to resuming his career in the foreign service after the charge that he had sex with a 14-year-old Cambodian boy was dimissed. Canberra Magistrate Michael Somes said in court the evidence from two Cambodian boys lacked credibility and had major inconsistencies. Page 1.
THE AGE

After being cleared of a child sex charge, former Ambassador to Cambodia, John Holloway, yesterday warned against "homophobic attacks" associated with the New South Wales Police Royal Commission and a Federal inquiry into paedophilia among diplomats in th Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Holloway also said the Child Sex Tourism Act, under which he was charged, provided foreign governments with a powerful weapon. Page A1.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has narrowly fought off a backbench revolt over legislation that will require people playing war games or paintball skirmish games to hold a shooter's licence from early next year. A motion overturning the decision was defeted by only five votes, but many believed a secret ballot would have led to the motion's success. Page A1.

Parliament heard yesterday the company Vipac Engineers and Scientists, awarded a Government industry grant last year, was associated with State Government MP Wendy Smith while she held the position as a senior ministerial adviser and her husband was a dirctor of Vipac. The Legislative Council's Opposition leader Theo Theophanous sought an assurance from Industry Minister Mark Birrell that the award was conducted with complete propriety and probity. Wendy Smith denied knowledge that her husband's companyhad applied for assistance under the scheme and that she had any influence regarding the decision. Page A3.

Japan's Ministry for Health and Welfare has launched an investigation into the food poisoning outbreak on 14 Qantas flights from Cairns to the Japanese cities of Tokyo, Sapporo, Fukuoka and Nagoya, after 348 passengers were struck ill by the flight. Japanese Health authorities revealed that 52 passengers were still in hospital from the incident. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
